Tallerico (a marxist-socialist-islamist), as well El Sayed in Michigan (an Islamist associated and funded by Muslim Brotherhood --Hamas terrorists), when objectively viewed, are among the most dangerous people on earth -- whose ultimate objective is the enslavement of everyone; to support the objectives of Islamic worship of their demon god and the destruction of all non-muslims (under a caliphate); or in the alternative, should the other side be savvy to the tactics of Islam (as was Egypt and China), the objective is the marxist-socialist goal of practical worship of the state (and the autocratic leaders).

In the end, where islamists are involved with conventional marxists-socialists who have no history or wisdom in dealing with Islamist treachery, they typically end up killing off the marxists-socialists, as they did in Iran, in Syria and in Lebanon.

This pattern of Islamic tactical infiltration to dominate and take control, is now playing out in the U.S., enabled by "useful idiots" who do not understand history and/or refuse to recognize the blatantly obvious before their eyes.

Far-left (marxist, socialist, communist, or anti-imperialist) groups and Islamists have repeatedly formed short-term partnerships against secular nationalists, or local authorities. They share enemies and some common framing (anti-imperialism, social justice rhetoric), but diverge sharply on core aims: class-based atheistic materialism versus theocratic rule under Islam Sharia.

Tactical alliances between leftists and Islamists against common enemies are typically temporary. When Islamists gain the upper hand, they typically sideline and eliminate leftist partners.

As noted, in the rare event where the non-muslim side is wise enough to take control, as in Egypt (still developing) and China, the dominant parties were savvy to the tactics of Islam and took steps to guard against their treachery.

ISLAMISTS DOMINATE
IRAN: A classic example is the 1979 Iranian Revolution, where leftists (including Tudeh communists) and secular nationalists allied with Khomeini’s Islamists against the Shah. Once in power, the Islamists purged and executed the leftists. In the 1979 revolution against the Shah, a broad coalition formed: leftists (including the Tudeh Party, Fedayeen guerrillas, and Mojahedin-e Khalq), secular nationalists, liberals, and Islamists under Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. Shared anti-imperialist and anti-Shah intersts drew them together. Individuals such as Ali Shariati had attempted intellectual syntheses of Islam and socialist ideas -- in futility (it has never been done where Islam has the upper hand. Once the monarchy fell, Khomeini and the clerical establishment rapidly consolidated control through the Islamic Republic and the doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist). Leftists and other non-Islamist revolutionaries were purged via arrests, university closures for “Islamification,” show trials, and executions—including mass killings of political prisoners in the early 1980s and the 1988 massacres. Many leftists had initially supported or tolerated Khomeini as the anti-imperialist vehicle; the Islamists discarded them once power was secured. This outcome awaits the U.S., where the Islamists now establishing mosques at a record pace around the country, largely share the IRGC ideology, and boldly preach jihad, hatred and death to non-muslims, and overthrow of the U.S. government.

LEBANON: During the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990), leftist forces (including the Lebanese National Movement and PLO elements) collaborated with emerging Shiite groups such as precursors of Hezbollah allied against Christians and other non-muslims. Hezbollah’s power stems primarily from Iranian sponsorship, Shia demographic weight, and military strength rather than Marxist partnership -- but it has not achieved a full takeover of the country due to Israeli involvement as a defensive measure against Hezbollah aggression. The intervention of Israel has stood in the breach to prevent darkness and destruction for all Lebanese.

SYRIA: In Syria, the ruling system until December 2024 was Ba’athist Arab socialism under the Assad family (Alawite-led). It blended pan-Arab nationalism, socialism (nationalizations, one-party rule, Soviet-style elements at times), and a secular style that treated Islam as a cultural heritage of the Arab nation rather than a theocratic system. It was never Islamist and was often hostile to the political Islam that is now gaining a foothold in the U.S. including such players as El Sayed, Omar, Tlaib and others -- due to assistance of useful idiots who do not see through their ideological treachery of domination and ultimate elimination of non-muslims. In late November–December 2024, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), led by Ahmad al-Sharaa, formerly Abu Mohammad al-Jolani; originally an al-Qaeda affiliate that rebranded) led a rapid offensive that captured Aleppo, Hama, Homs, and Damascus. Assad fled to Russia. HTS dominates the subsequent interim authorities. This constitutes an Islamist-led overthrow of the long-ruling Ba’athist socialist-nationalist regime. This is what the Islamists in the U.S have in mind -- following the pattern of what was done in Iran.

Similar modern era outcomes in other nations have arisen through military coups or conquest (Afghanistan, Sudan), institutional capture and legal Islamization (Pakistan under Zia), and elsewhere at various stages of social chaos, political unrest and ensuing disaster.

SOCIALISTS PREDOMINATE
EGYPT: In Egypt, Ba’athist and Nasserist regimes were the main vehicles of “Arab socialism.” They were secular-nationalist and often brutal toward Islamists. After the 2011 revolution, Mohamed Morsi (Muslim Brotherhood) took power in 2012 before a 2013 military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. The current regime is a secular-nationalist military authoritarian system that has, with the wisdom of Solomon, cracked down on both Islamists and independent leftists.

CHINA: In China, Hui (Sinophone) Muslim units joined the People’s Liberation Army that fought as part of communist or communist-aligned forces. The CCP initially used united-front tactics, recognized Hui as a nationality, and offered limited cultural concessions early on to gain support against warlords and the KM (later fleeing to Taiwan). After 1949, the CCP authoritarian governance was successful in systematically subordinating and suppressing Islam and to a lesser degree, other religious groups -- as the CCP recognized early on, that Islamic ideology (Sharia) and Qur’anic based aggressive (or suicidal) end time eschatology was diametrically opposed to any other form of government. CCP Policies under the broad scope of land reform, the Socialist Education Movement, the Cultural Revolution led to destruction of mosques, persecution of muslim practitioners, the 1975 Shadian incident in Yunnan (massacre of roughly 1,600 Muslim civilians), and assimilation campaigns, especially toward Uyghurs in Xinjiang. The CCP turned the legacy Islamist tactic of infiltrate and conquer -- now in play in the U.S -- on its head, insofar as their early tolerance was tactical; whereas the long-term direction was secularization and elimination of Islam and complete CCP control (whereas Islam would otherwise have eventually eliminated the Maoists).

text:
The View from Oregon – 415
Re: Testing the Presuppositions of Counting
Friday 16 October 2026

Dear Friends,

There’s a passage from Karl Popper’s Conjectures and Refutations that I like to quote about observation in science. I recently quoted this in my episode on the 18 June 1178 lunar impact (or whatever it was that was witnessed that medieval summer by a handful of men looking up at the moon):

“…I tried to bring home the same point to a group of physics students in Vienna by beginning a lecture with the following instructions : ‘Take pencil and paper; carefully observe, and write down what you have observed!’ They asked, of course, what I wanted them to observe. Clearly the instruction, ‘Observe!’ is absurd… Observation is always selective. It needs a chosen object, a definite task, an interest, a point of view, a problem. And its description presupposes a descriptive language, with property words; it presupposes similarity and classification, which in their turn presuppose interests, points of view, and problems.”

I take this to be one of the most important things that Popper wrote; more important than his falsifiability criterion as a test for science, and more important than anything in The Poverty of Historicism or The Open Society and Its Enemies (both of which I once admired, but which I now view less favorably).

One of the formal counterparts to observation is counting. In order to count, we can’t just issue the imperative, “Count, and write down the number you have counted.” Or, rather, we can do this, but the results would vary as widely as issuing the imperative to observe without also being sufficiently selective about what is to be observed. In the case of counting, we must be sufficiently selective about what is to be counted. Counting, like observation, needs a chosen object, a definite task, an interest, a point of view, and a problem. Our counting, no less than our observing, is motivated, and we get the best results by being explicit about our motivations.

Some qualifications are in order, however. Popper was discussing scientific observation in the passage I quoted above, but not all observation is scientific. It is actually quite common in life for someone to say, “Watch now!” which is usually taken to mean that something interesting is about to happen momentarily so that we should pay especially careful attention, and, if we do, whatever it is we were intended to observe, will be obvious to us when the moment arrives. We wait with expectation that something of note will occur in the near future. Say, for example, we are taken to an especially elaborate astronomical clock, and, as the hour is about to strike, we are told, “Observe now!” And, in fact, when the hour strikes we are entertained by the procession of figures that turn and dance and ring bells, and so on. There’s nothing at all ambiguous about this, but, in all fairness, it’s not scientific observation that is focused on solving a problem.

Just so with counting. We can be asked to count, and the circumstances are sufficiently clear that we gain of sense of what we are to count from the context of the imperative to count. But, as obvious as the context may be to some, the context will not be as obvious for others. I can think of many times in my own life when I was asked to perform some simple task that the person asking thought was entirely obvious, and I misunderstood, sometimes misunderstanding both the task and the reason for the task, and, with this personal experience of my own fallibility, I tend to view all such requests as being riddled with ambiguity when presented without a considerable measure of clarification. No doubt I have gained a reputation of being particularly pig-headed about insisting on explicit and full instructions, but experience has taught me that, without sufficient instructions, the whole effort is a failure and a waste of time for all involved. One of the obvious problems is that those who assume that context will supply what is missing in any incomplete instructions fail to recognize that the ultimate context is the entire life of the other person, and, beyond that, the history of the culture in which the individual is acculturated, and the evolutionary history of the species (and I will return to this). Even though the difference between any two individuals seems negligible, so that we don’t have to account for the context supplied by the entire life of another individual, human beings, despite our overwhelming similarity, have incommensurably distinct experiences.

There is something to be learned from this ambiguity, however. Or, rather, there is something to be investigated in this ambiguity. Both observation and counting could be a wonderful opportunity to engage in what is now called experimental philosophy. Intuitions as to what is obvious vary among individuals, but this variation may cluster, and it may cluster in predictable patterns. If so, this could be discovered by experimental philosophy that sought to determine what is most effectively observed or counted when instructions are purposefully left ambiguous, and how they are left ambiguous. For example, one could display a tray with several items on it, but also have a patterned repetitious decoration on the tray, so that the experimental subject in being asked to count when shown the tray, might count the items on the tray, or the iterations in the patterns on the tray, or maybe even count the tray itself as one and stop there. This is only a single example. A thorough research program of experimental philosophy in individuation and countability would need to formulate a wide variety of ambiguous scenarios, preferably based on some taxonomy of ambiguity (like J. L. Austin’s seven types of vagueness in Sense and Sensibility) so as to control separately for each kind of ambiguity. We would also have to control for differences in context, since, as I mentioned above, the assumption is often that context supplies the disambiguation of incomplete instructions.

In such an experiment in counting, we are converging (hopefully we are converging) on intuitions about individuality and countability, which are closely related. These intuitions could vary culturally, or among species, or among intelligences. Ideally we would run the counting experiment with many distinct forms of intelligence. Beyond the intelligence of the individual, characteristic as it is of the species to which the individual belongs, there is the larger complexity regime that the intelligence in question represents. Since I’ve been talking about ambiguity here, let me be a little more explicit about the tripartite distinction I’m making in regard to forms that intelligence can take:

1. A distinction among individuals of the same species, according to which cultural differences could correspond to differences as to what constitutes individuality and countability.

2. A distinction among different species within the same biosphere, but all species in question belonging to the same tree of life, according to which intelligence may be expressed differently, translating into different conceptions of individuality and countability.

3. A distinction among intelligent beings derived from different trees of life, and possibility even derived from different complexity regimes, according to which intelligence could once again be expressed differently in different intuitions of individuation and countability.

Given the large themes this tripartite distinction addresses, we might want to narrow in on a few explicitly formulated problems, so that we have, as Popper said, a definite task, an interest, a point of view, and a problem. A principle could be posited according to which each complexity regime admits of a single form of intelligence. This intelligence may be represented poorly or optimally by any given individual who belongs to the complexity regime in question, but it is nevertheless the same kind of intelligence in every case that is represented. If a given biosphere (or, more generally, for non-biological complexity regimes, a given chemosphere) gives rise to multiple intelligences, then, according to this hypothesis, these intelligences will all be of the same form. Again, this form of intelligence might be represented well or poorly, or with particular partial representations characteristic of the ecology of the species in question (its place in the trophic pyramid, i.e., in the food web), but all are variations on the same given kind of intelligence.

This hypothesis has significant consequences for what I have called intelligence-rich biospheres, which would be a biosphere (or, again, a chemosphere for non-biological complexity regimes) in which more than one human-level intelligence evolves. I explored intelligence-rich biospheres in a number of thought experiments that I wrote up as blog posts some years ago. I rather like this thought experiment; each time I return to it I discover another aspect to the problem that hadn’t occurred to me previously, and so I find thinking about the possibility of intelligence-rich biospheres to be philosophically fruitful. Now I find I’ve come at this from yet another angle, and so I now have yet another way to think about intelligence-rich biospheres. And the hypothesis that I’ve proposed in this newsletter on the taxonomic unity of intelligence within a given complexity regime suggests the possibility of a counter-hypothesis such that a given complexity regime might have more than one or many forms of intelligence, or it might be incompatible with any kind of intelligence at all.

If a given biosphere or complexity regime can produce many fundamentally different kinds of intelligence, then the kind intelligence that arises in consequence of increasing complexity within a given complexity regime is not coupled to the evolutionary history of the intelligent being in question. That is to say, the evolutionary process that yielded an intelligent being was not fated by the nature of that complexity regime to produce one and only one specific kind of intelligence; a given complexity regime can be consistent with a number of fundamentally distinct kinds of intelligence. If, in a very different scenario, all intelligence is essentially the same despite whatever complexity regime upon which it supervenes, then there is only one kind of intelligence. Both of these scenarios point to intelligence as being strongly convergent, but the first points to intelligence converging on a type defined by the complexity regime upon which it supervenes (which is a form of path dependency), while the second scenario points to intelligence always converging on a universal type that is everywhere and always the same, independent of its substrate, and therefore, in a sense, a law unto itself. Again, this universal intelligence might be poorly or optimally represented, or it may be partially or comprehensively represented, which gives the appearance of a variety of kinds of intelligence, but which, according to this hypothesis, are nevertheless essentially all of the same kind of intelligence.

Not only does this series of questions have important consequences for my intelligence-rich biosphere thought experiments of some years ago, it also has implications for the several newsletters I wrote earlier this year about the kinds of and classifications for intelligence. And, again, as with intelligence-rich biospheres, it provides another approach to this problem which may offer new insights from the fresh perspective adopted. If only we had the experimental subjects available to us, we could design a comprehensive research program in experimental philosophy that could at least partially answer some of the questions posed by the possibility of qualitatively distinct forms of intelligence.

Best wishes,

Nick

PS—After a month on Kalymnos, arriving in Thessaloniki is so different that I can’t place the two experiences in the same continuum; living on an island and visiting a city are nearly incommensurable experiences. Thessaloniki has a long waterfront that’s all sea wall—a wide promenade with no railing or balustrade, a few benches (not many), a lot of pedestrians, and the occasional individual fishing. Directly across the road that parallels the promenade is one open air café after another, which, given their situation, all have a view over the bay. They’re all packed with people. Evidently the Thessalonikians value their café culture. This is the area between the ferry terminal and the White Tower. At the White Tower the waterfront makes a turn and continues on for much longer, with fewer cafés and more benches, and a lot of trees that shade the benches, so it’s a nice place to sit and relax and take in the view. It’s a very long waterfront. You can easily walk for an hour and not cover it all. I know because I walked an hour along the waterfront to get to the ethnographic museum, which was closed when I got there, but in my hour’s walk I didn’t exhaust the waterfront. It was a beautiful walk. Most of the major museums are quite close to the White Tower—the Museum of Byzantine Culture (my primary reason for visiting Thessaloniki) and the archaeological museum are a few minutes’ walk from here. There’s also a large equestrian statue of Alexander the Great on the waterfront near the White Tower (which isn’t white, by the way).
